shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: In 1995, the average person in Portugal produced almost twice as much as the average person in Poland, adjusted for prices. {p} Portugal had been in the European Union for almost a decade. Poland had just escaped communism. {p} In 2020, when the pandemic emptied Portugal's hotels, Poland pulled ahead. Portugal clawed its way back in 2023. {pp} In 2025, Poland passed it again, by about two percent, and this time no pandemic was needed.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $) · Eurostat prc_ppp_ind (actual individual consumption per head, PPS, 2024)
shots.title: Who passed Portugal
shots.narration: Poland isn't the first. {p} Slovenia has been ahead for good since 2003. Czechia since 2007. Malta since 2009. Lithuania since 2018. {p} And three more are within about five percent: Estonia, Romania and Croatia. {pp} By one measure of how people actually live, what they consume per person, Romanians are already slightly ahead.

Portugal isn't poor. It's a rich, safe, beautiful country that a lot of people dream of moving to. {p} But for twenty-five years, it barely got richer, while its neighbors to the east sprinted. {p} This isn't a story about a country failing. It's about standing still while everyone around you runs. {p} So what happened to Portugal? {pp} <soft>And is it as bad as it looks?</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), change since 1990
shots.narration: It wasn't always like this. {p} After Portugal joined the European Union in 1986, it was catching up fast. {p} From 1990 to 2000, its output per person grew about twenty-nine percent, adjusted for prices. The EU's grew about twenty. {pp} Then, right around the year 2000, something broke.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), change since 2000
shots.narration: Look at growth since then. {p} From 2000 to 2025, output per person in Lithuania has roughly tripled. In Poland, it's grown about two and a half times. Romania's, almost as much. {p} The EU as a whole: up more than a third. {p} Portugal? {pp} Up about a fifth. In twenty-five years. Only Greece, crushed by its own debt crisis, did about as badly.

And that's not just the pandemic. {p} From 2000 to 2019, Portugal's output per person grew just fifteen percent. {p} That's less than one percent a year, for almost two decades. Poland managed that much growth in less than four years. {p} Even Spain, next door, grew a little faster. {p} In 2000, Portugal was at about eighty-five percent of the EU average in output per person. By 2015, it had slipped to about seventy-six. {pp} <soft>For a generation of Portuguese, the economy simply stood still.</soft>

shots.src: Eurostat edat_lfse_03 · adults 25–64 with at least upper secondary education (%)
shots.narration: The biggest reason is one most people never think about: school. {p} In 2000, fewer than one in five Portuguese adults had finished high school. {p} In Poland, four in five. In Czechia and Lithuania, more than eight in ten. {p} That's a legacy of the dictatorship that ended in 1974, which kept schooling short for most people. {p} Portugal entered the global economy with a workforce built for farms and small workshops. {pp} Today it's at about two in three, and climbing fast.

shots.src: WTO (China accession, 11 Dec 2001) · EU enlargement (1 May 2004) · European Commission, financial assistance to Portugal (2011–2014): €78 billion EU/IMF programme
shots.title: Then came the shocks
shots.narration: Then came the shocks. {p} In 2001, China joined the World Trade Organization. In 2004, eight countries from Central and Eastern Europe joined the EU. {p} Both offered what Portugal sold: cheap labor for textiles, shoes and assembly. {p} And inside the euro, Portugal could no longer devalue its currency to stay competitive. {p} When the euro crisis hit, Portugal needed a seventy-eight billion euro bailout in 2011.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · gross fixed capital formation, % of GDP · net migration (SM.POP.NETM)
shots.narration: The bailout came with deep cuts. {p} Investment collapsed to about fifteen percent of the economy, among the lowest in the European Union. {p} And between 2011 and 2014, Portugal lost more than a hundred and thirty thousand people to emigration, net. {pp} Fewer machines, fewer workers, <soft>and a lost decade on top of a lost decade.</soft>
Quick favor: if you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, here's where people actually feel it: {pp} the paycheck.

shots.src: Eurostat earn_mw_cur · monthly minimum wage, € (adjusted to 12 payments a year)
shots.narration: In 2005, Portugal's minimum wage was about four hundred and forty euros a month. Poland's: about two hundred and ten. Less than half. {p} In 2025, Portugal's was about one thousand and fifteen euros, counting the two extra payments Portuguese workers get each year. {p} Poland's: about eleven hundred. Lithuania's: more than a thousand. {pp} Both now higher than Portugal's. {p} For the lowest-paid Pole, that's about eighty-five euros more a month than for the lowest-paid Portuguese.

shots.src: Observatório da Emigração (via Expresso / Essential Business, 12 Jan 2024)
shots.title: Young Portuguese living abroad
shots.narration: No wonder so many leave. {p} By the Emigration Observatory's estimate, around eight hundred and fifty thousand people born in Portugal, aged fifteen to thirty-nine, live abroad. {pp} That's about thirty percent of that whole generation.

stats.label: of everyone born in Portugal, aged 15–39

shots.src: Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · actual individual consumption per head, PPS (EU = 100), 2024
shots.title: What people consume per head (EU = 100)
shots.narration: And remember Romania? {p} Eurostat measures what households actually consume, food, housing, and services the state provides, like health care and schools, adjusted for prices, against an EU average of one hundred. {p} In 2024, Portugal scores eighty-five. {pp} Romania scores eighty-eight. Lithuania, eighty-nine. {p} In 2000, Romania was at thirty.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · life expectancy at birth (years)
shots.narration: But GDP isn't everything. {p} The average Portuguese can expect to live about eighty-two years, longer than the average German. {p} In Poland, about seventy-eight. In Romania, about seventy-six and a half. {pp} Four to six extra years of life don't show up in output per person.

shots.src: Eurostat gov_10dd_edpt1 · government balance and debt, % of GDP (April 2026 notification)
shots.narration: And look at the public finances. {p} In 2025, Portugal ran a budget surplus for the third year in a row. {p} Poland ran a deficit of more than seven percent of its economy. Romania, almost eight, the largest in the EU. Even Greece now runs a surplus. {p} Portugal's government debt has fallen from a hundred and thirty-four percent of GDP in 2020 to about eighty-nine.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · net migration, Portugal (SM.POP.NETM)
shots.narration: And people are coming in again. {p} After losing more than a hundred and thirty thousand people in four crisis years, Portugal has had more arrivals than departures every year since 2017. {p} In 2021 alone, about seventy thousand more people moved in than left.

Since 2022, Portugal has grown faster than the EU average every single year. Unemployment, above sixteen percent in 2013, is back near six. {p} The tortoise, it turns out, kept its savings. {pp} <soft>Some of the hares are running on credit.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $), as % of Portugal
shots.narration: Still, the race isn't over. {p} In 2000, Romania produced about a third as much per person as Portugal. Estonia, about half. Croatia, under sixty percent. {p} Today it's at about ninety-six percent. Croatia, which only joined the EU in 2013, is at ninety-six too, and Estonia at about ninety-eight. {pp} The next few years will decide whether Portugal holds that line.

shots.src: Chartbound calculation: Eurostat GDP per capita in PPS (Portugal 2024 = 82% of EU), catching up 1 point per year faster than the EU
shots.title: To reach the EU average
shots.narration: And catching up is slow. {p} Portugal is at about eighty-two percent of the EU average in output per person. {p} Even if it grew one percentage point faster than the EU, every single year, {pp} it would take about twenty years to close the gap.

Portugal has done the hard part. {p} It rebuilt its schools, fixed its budget, and became a place people move to, not just from. {p} The question for the next twenty-five years is simple: {pp} <soft>can it finally turn all that into higher pay, before more of its young people leave to find it elsewhere?</soft> {p} Growth isn't everything. But over twenty-five years, it decides what a country can afford.
Poland didn't stop at Portugal. In 2026, it passed Japan too, and almost nobody noticed. To see how, watch the next video. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Just Passed Portugal. Again.
yt.description:
In 1995 the average Portuguese produced almost twice as much as the average Pole, adjusted for prices. Poland pulled ahead in the 2020–2022 pandemic years, Portugal clawed back in 2023, and in 2025 Poland passed it again. Slovenia, Czechia and Lithuania have been ahead for years, and Romanians already consume slightly more per head. Why Portugal stood still for 25 years (school, the China and EU-enlargement shocks, the 2011 bailout), what it means for wages, and the twist: longer lives, budget surpluses and a comeback since 2022.

Sources: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS, SM.POP.NETM, SP.DYN.LE00.IN, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG); Eurostat (prc_ppp_ind, edat_lfse_03, earn_mw_cur, gov_10dd_edpt1); European Commission (financial assistance to Portugal); WTO; EU enlargement 2004.
